text: The United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has filed an annual report pursuant to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, under Form 10-K. The registrant, The AES Corporation, is incorporated in the state of Delaware and has an IRS Employer Identification Number of 54-1163725. Its principal executive offices are located at 4300 Wilson Boulevard, Arlington, Virginia 22203, and its telephone number is (703) 522-1315. The company’s common stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol AES, and its corporate units trade under the symbol AESC. The AES Corporation is classified as a well-known seasoned issuer and is not required to file reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Act. It has filed all required reports during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to these filing requirements for the past 90 days. The company has submitted electronically all Interactive Data Files required under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T. It is designated as a large accelerated filer and has not elected not to use the extended transition period for financial accounting standards. The registrant has filed a report on and received an attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. There are no restatements of previously issued financial statements or corrections of errors requiring a recovery analysis of incentive-based compensation for executive officers. The company is not a shell company. As of June 30, 2022, the aggregate market value of the voting and non-voting common equity held by non-affiliates was approximately $14.03 billion, based on a closing sale price of $21.01 per share on the New York Stock Exchange. The number of shares outstanding of the company’s common stock, par value $0.01 per share, as of February 27, 2023, was 668,824,617. Portions of the registrant’s 2023 Proxy Statement are incorporated by reference in Parts II and III of the report. The document includes a Table of Contents with a Glossary of Terms, and the report covers various sections including Business, Risk Factors, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Market for Common Equity, Selected Financial Data, Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations, Market Risk, Financial Statements, and related notes. Additionally, the report includes disclosures on changes in accountants, controls and procedures, and other information.

The 2022 Annual Report includes various financial notes and disclosures, such as Note 24 on Held-for-Sale and Dispositions, Note 25 on Acquisitions, Note 26 on Earnings Per Share, Note 27 on Risks and Uncertainties, Note 28 on Related Party Transactions, Note 29 on Selected Quarterly Financial Data (Unaudited), and Note 30 on Subsequent Events. It also covers specific sections including Item 9 on Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants, Item 9A on Controls and Procedures, Item 9B on Other Information, and Item 9C on Foreign Jurisdictions Preventing Inspections. Part III includes Item 10 on Directors, Executive Officers, and Corporate Governance, Item 11 on Executive Compensation, Item 12 on Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management, Item 13 on Certain Relationships and Related Party Transactions and Director Independence, and Item 14 on Principal Accountant Fees and Services. Part IV, Item 15, contains Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules. The report defines key terms such as ACED, AES, Adjusted EPS, Adjusted PTC, AFUDC, AIMCo, ANEEL, AOCL, ARO, ASC, BACT, BESS, BOT, CAA, CAMMESA, CCEE, CCGT, CCR, CDPQ, CECL, CEO, CFE, CFO, CO, COD, CSAPR, CWA, DG, DPL, DPP, EPA, EPC, ERCOT, ESP, EU, EURIBOR, EVN, FERC, Fluence, FONINVEMEM, FPA, FX, GAAP, GHG, GILTI, GSF, GW, GWh, HLBV. The report defines "AES," "the Company," "us," or "we" as referring to The AES Corporation and all of its subsidiaries and affiliates, while "The AES Corporation" and "Parent Company" refer only to the parent holding company, excluding subsidiaries and affiliates. Forward-looking statements are included in the report and are considered within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially due to factors such as the economic climate in operating regions and China, fluctuations in electricity prices and the effectiveness of risk management practices, changes in fuel prices and availability (including coal, gas, and transportation), access to financial markets and capital costs, inflation, demand for power, interest rates, and foreign exchange rates, the ability to meet debt obligations and manage liquidity, the receipt of funds from subsidiaries, and changes in corporate or subsidiary credit ratings.

AES is a global energy company founded in 1981, committed to delivering greener, smarter energy solutions and improving lives through innovation and operational excellence. The company is an industry leader in advancing zero and low-carbon energy solutions to achieve the Paris Agreement’s net-zero emissions goal by 2050. AES focuses on partnering with large corporations transitioning to carbon-free electricity, as evidenced by being recognized in 2022 by BNEF as the #1 global clean energy developer for corporations. In 2022, the company signed long-term contracts for 5.2 GW of renewable power, increasing its project backlog—comprising signed but not yet operational projects—to 12.2 GW, which serves as the foundation for future growth. A key element of its strategy is customer collaboration and co-creation, enabling tailored energy solutions that enhance customer satisfaction and allow bilateral partnerships beyond traditional bidding processes. This approach led to innovations such as agreements to supply 24/7 carbon-free energy for global data centers and a partnership with Air Products to develop and operate the largest green hydrogen production facility in the United States. AES also supports major mining companies in South America in reducing emissions through its Green Blend offering, which integrates renewable energy with thermal power to lower emissions. In its utility operations, AES promotes a Just Transition by retiring coal generation, such as at AES Indiana, where coal operations will be fully retired by the end of 2025, while adding new renewables and natural gas. The company expanded its development pipeline from 55 GW in January 2022 to 64 GW by the end of 2022 through acquisitions and increased investment in land acquisition and permitting. To mitigate supply chain risks, AES secured supplier arrangements for late-stage projects using its scale and advanced planning. A significant portion of its capital expenditures through 2025 will be allocated to renewable energy development. AES also operates AES Next, a business and technology incubator focused on identifying innovative technologies and business opportunities that support greener energy solutions. In 2022, the company signed 5,153 MW of long-term contracts. The company’s operations and future performance are subject to a range of risks, including market price risk, fuel availability and transportation, financial market conditions, inflation, interest rates, foreign exchange rates, liquidity and debt covenants, dividend and fund receipt capabilities, credit ratings, asset purchase and sale terms, competitive dynamics, facility operations, maintenance costs, contract performance, weather and natural disasters, pandemics, supply chain disruptions, capital availability, renewable project success, government incentives, environmental, social, and governance performance, technological advancements, customer trends, joint venture performance, rate treatment, regulatory changes, environmental laws, tax laws, litigation, acquisition performance, insurance, pension plan funding, asset impairments, accounting standards, internal controls, talent retention, cyber-attacks, and data privacy. These factors, along with others detailed in Item 1A.—Risk Factors and subsequent filings, should not be considered a comprehensive list of potential risks. AES undertakes no obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements, whether due to new information or future events.

Our renewable growth strategy focuses on ensuring and enabling future growth by significantly expanding our pipeline of development projects, which increased from 55 GW in January 2022 to 64 GW by the end of 2022 through acquisitions and greater investment in development activities such as securing land and advancing permitting and interconnection processes. For late-stage projects, we secured supplier arrangements to prevent delays caused by industry shortages, leveraging our scale, existing supplier relationships, and advanced planning. A large portion of our expected capital expenditures through 2025 will be allocated to renewable project development. We are also actively developing and incubating new technologies that deliver value today and will support future business growth, recognizing the rapid changes in the energy industry. At the core of our innovation strategy is AES Next, a business and technology incubator that identifies innovative technologies and business opportunities to advance leading-edge, greener energy solutions. In 2022, we signed 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage under long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), including 2,553 MW of solar, wind, and energy storage in the United States. We completed the construction or acquisition of 1,943 MW of operating projects in the United States, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Chile, and Colombia, primarily in wind, solar, and energy storage. Our backlog—comprising projects with signed contracts but not yet operational—stands at 12,179 MW, including 5,453 MW under construction and 6,726 MW with signed PPAs not yet under construction. We announced a partnership with Air Products to develop, build, own, and operate the largest green hydrogen production facility in the United States, which includes approximately 1.4 GW of wind and solar generation and electrolyzer capacity capable of producing over 200 metric tons per day (MT/D) of green hydrogen. The company also expects to announce internal management changes that will result in modifications to its financial reporting segments. Our generation portfolio consists of 32,326 MW, including operations from AES Indiana, and is diversified by fuel type. Key performance drivers include types of electricity sales agreements, plant reliability and flexibility, availability of generation capacity, fuel costs, seasonality, weather variations, economic activity, fixed-cost management, and competition. Most generation businesses sell electricity under medium- or long-term contracts (two to five years or more than five years), with contracts for fuel-based generation structured to recover variable costs through pass-throughs or tolling arrangements. Contracts without fuel pass-throughs are typically hedged or supported by fuel or energy supply agreements, and many include capacity payments to cover fixed costs such as fixed O&M, debt service, and a return on capital, often denominated in the same currency as fixed costs. Contracts without significant fuel costs or capacity payments are based on long-term spot prices with negotiated pass-throughs to recover fixed and variable costs and provide a return on investment. We generally eliminate or reduce foreign exchange risk by matching revenue and expense currencies, including fixed costs and debt, and hedge a significant portion of exposure to interest rate changes. Project debt may include both fixed and floating rates. Some businesses receive regulated market-based capacity payments. In short-term sales, power and ancillary services are sold under contracts with average terms under two years, including spot sales in competitive markets or at regulated prices. These markets operate on merit order dispatch, where the least expensive generation facilities are dispatched first, and prices are typically set at marginal cost or bid price. These businesses are more sensitive to electricity price fluctuations. We provide a range of ancillary services, including voltage support, frequency regulation, and spinning reserves. Many short-term markets include regulated capacity markets, which provide additional revenue based on availability, priced based on new entrant costs and system reserve margin. Capacity payments are typically received based on plant availability. Contract and short-term sales incentivize plants to manage availability, efficiency, and flexibility. For thermal generation, fuel is a major cost component; we use fuel supply agreements or financial hedges to manage costs, with some contracts including indexation, and tolling arrangements where off-takers cover fuel supply and costs. In short-term sales, power is sold at market prices reflecting current fuel costs, and fuel is procured on a short-term basis to match sales. Fuel price volatility significantly impacts short-term project economics. Forty-six percent of our generation capacity is fueled by renewables—including hydro, solar, wind, energy storage, biomass, and landfill gas—without significant fuel costs. Thirty-two percent is fueled by natural gas, with the exception of plants in the Dominican Republic and Panama, which import liquefied natural gas (LNG); otherwise, we source gas from local suppliers. Twenty percent of our fleet is coal-fired; in the U.S., most coal is sourced domestically, while in non-U.S. plants and Puerto Rico, coal is sourced from international and local markets, with global sourcing used to maximize fuel procurement efficiency. Twenty percent of its generation fleet's capacity is coal-fired, with domestic coal sourced in the U.S., while in non-U.S. plants and in Puerto Rico, coal is obtained from a mix of international and local sources. The company leverages its global sourcing program to enhance fuel procurement purchasing power. Two percent of the generation fleet uses pet coke, diesel, or oil, with oil and diesel sourced locally at prices tied to international markets, and pet coke primarily sourced from Mexico and the U.S. Generation operations are influenced by seasonal weather patterns, leading to uneven operating margins throughout the year, as well as by weather variations such as temperature, solar and wind resources, and hydrological conditions, which affect output at renewable facilities. In competitive power markets, local economic activity impacts power demand and short-term prices. For businesses with long-term contracts, most fixed operations and maintenance (O&M) costs are recovered through capacity payments, though managing and reducing fixed costs over time remains a key driver of performance. In medium- or long-term contracts, competition is limited during the contract term; short-term sales, plant dispatch, and electricity prices are determined by market competition and local dispatch and reliability rules. The company’s utility businesses include AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. and four utilities in El Salvador, serving 2.6 million customers, with the two U.S. utilities also including 3,495 MW of generation capacity. AES Indiana, a fully integrated utility, owns and operates all facilities for generation, transmission, and distribution, while AES Ohio owns and operates only transmission and distribution facilities. In El Salvador, the distribution business faces limited competition due to market entry barriers, and large regulated customers can opt to become unregulated and purchase directly from generation or commercialization agents. Utilities generally sell electricity directly to end-users and bill them directly; key performance drivers include the regulated rate of return and tariff, seasonality, weather variations, economic activity, and service reliability. Utilities are subject to government regulation, which sets tariffs and service standards, allowing a regulated rate of return on assets based on the utility’s allowed regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital. The asset base reflects the amount of useful assets serving customers, and both the allowed return and asset base are critical to earning power. The regulated tariff recovers allowed operating expenses and fixed costs, including fuel and purchased energy costs, and may include pass-throughs of uncontrollable costs. Tariffs are periodically reviewed or reset by regulators, often based on usage levels, and in some regions, customers with high demand can bypass the tariff by contracting directly with generators or suppliers and paying non-bypassable fees for distribution system use. Utilities must manage costs to match those in the tariff to avoid non-recovery or reduced returns. Seasonality and weather variations also affect utility operations, with retail sales influenced by customer usage patterns, temperature deviations, and local economic conditions, including energy efficiency and distributed generation. Reliability standards, such as outage duration and frequency, are required, either explicitly with performance incentives or penalties or implicitly through meeting customer and regulator expectations. The company develops and constructs new generation facilities, with utility projects built or retrofitted in response to customer needs or regulatory changes, subject to regulatory approval for capital recovery and return on investment. For generation, development priorities focus on key growth markets where renewable energy is added to leverage global scale and synergies with existing operations. Investment decisions are based on strategic fit, project returns, financial profile, and a fair risk-adjusted return, compared to alternative capital uses such as debt repayment. In some cases, long-term output contracts are secured before construction begins to reduce equity contributions from The AES Corporation, with non-recourse project debt and other capital sources, including partners, used when commercially viable. Third parties typically manage construction, though the company’s construction management team oversees progress, budget, and adherence to safety, efficiency, and productivity standards. The company is organized into four market-oriented strategic business units (SBUs): US and Utilities (U.S., Puerto Rico, and El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe and Asia), led by SBU Presidents. The two primary lines of business are generation and utilities. Each SBU participates in generation, where the company owns or operates power plants to generate and sell electricity to utilities, industrial users, and intermediaries. The US and Utilities SBU also participates in utilities, where it owns or operates utilities to generate, purchase, distribute, transmit, and sell electricity to residential, commercial, industrial, and government customers within defined service areas. In certain cases, utilities also generate and sell electricity on the wholesale market. SBU performance is measured using Adjusted PTC, a non-GAAP metric. AES Indiana is an integrated utility that generates, transmits, distributes, and sells electric energy to retail customers in Indianapolis and surrounding areas in Indiana, serving approximately 971,000 people across about 528 square miles. It holds an exclusive right to provide electric service in this area and operates four generating stations—all located within Indiana. The largest, Petersburg, is coal-fired; AES Indiana retired 230 MW of Petersburg Unit 1 on May 31, 2021, and plans to retire 415 MW of Petersburg Unit 2 in 2023, resulting in a total of 630 MW of retired economic capacity at the station. AES Indiana intends to convert the remaining two coal units at Petersburg to natural gas by the end of 2025. The second-largest station, Harding Street, uses natural gas and fuel oil to power combustion turbines and includes a 20 MW battery-based energy storage unit that provides frequency response. Eagle Valley is a CCGT natural gas plant, and Georgetown is a small peaking station using natural gas combustion turbines. AES Indiana also meets customer energy needs through long-term contracts for 300 MW of wind-generated electricity and 94 MW of solar-generated electricity. In July 2021, AES Indiana entered into an agreement to acquire a 250 MW solar and 180 MWh energy storage facility, the "Petersburg Solar Project," which was amended in October 2022 and is now expected to be completed in 2025, subject to IURC approval. In December 2021, AES Indiana completed the acquisition of Hardy Hills Solar Energy LLC, including a 195 MW solar project, the "Hardy Hills Solar Project," which was amended in December 2022 and is now expected to be completed in 2024, subject to IURC approval. AES Indiana's financial performance is primarily influenced by retail demand, weather, and maintenance costs, as well as regulatory outcomes, changes in legislation or regulations, and the timely recovery of capital expenditures. The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) regulates AES Indiana’s services, rates, securities issuance, and other matters, setting tariff rates that include basic rates and approved charges, along with various adjustment mechanisms such as the Fuel Adjustment Charge, environmental compliance costs, RTO cost changes, wholesale sales margins, returns on eligible TDSIC investments, and demand-side management program recoveries. On October 31, 2018, the IURC approved a settlement increasing AES Indiana’s annual revenues by $44 million (3%), primarily due to costs from the Eagle Valley CCGT and other construction projects, with new rates effective December 5, 2018. This order, the most recent base rate order, provided customers with approximately $50 million in benefits over two years through rate adjustments. AES Indiana is a member of MISO, a regional transmission organization that manages a major energy and ancillary services market and dispatches generation assets to meet demand, with AES Indiana offering electricity in MISO’s day-ahead and real-time markets. Its development strategy includes capital expenditures for utility operations and environmental compliance, as well as discretionary investments to replace aging equipment or improve performance. The TDSIC statute (Senate Enrolled Act 560) allows cost recovery outside base rate proceedings for transmission, distribution, and storage projects aimed at safety, reliability, modernization, or economic development. Eligible projects must include a five-year to seven-year plan, and once approved by the IURC, 80% of eligible costs can be recovered via a periodic TDSIC rate adjustment mechanism, including a return on investment, AFUDC, post-in-service carrying charges, operations, maintenance, depreciation, and property taxes, with the remaining 20% deferred to the next base rate case. The TDSIC mechanism is capped at a two percent annual increase of total retail revenues. On March 4, 2020, the IURC approved AES Indiana’s seven-year TDSIC Plan, totaling $1.2 billion in eligible investments from 2020 through 2026. Beginning in June 2020, AES Indiana files annual TDSIC rate adjustments for returns on investments through March 31, with rates effective each November, and submits annual plan updates staggered by six months, filed each December. As of December 31, 2022, the total amount of equipment approved for TDSIC recovery was $324 million. In December 2022, AES Indiana filed its Integrated Resource Plan (IRP), which outlines its preferred resource portfolio for meeting future generation needs, representing the reasonable least cost option and a cleaner, more diverse energy mix. AES Indiana plans to transition its remaining coal units at Petersburg to natural gas by the end of 2025. Although AES Indiana has not yet filed for regulatory approvals from the IURC to convert Petersburg Units 3 and 4, it expects to file at the appropriate time. The company also intends to add up to 1,300 MW of wind, solar, and battery energy storage by 2027. As new technologies such as green hydrogen, small modular reactors, and carbon capture become cost-effective, AES Indiana will evaluate them in future planning processes. AES Indiana's 2019 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) included the retirement of 230 MW of Petersburg Unit 1 on May 31, 2021, and a plan to retire 415 MW of Petersburg Unit 2 in 2023. In November 2021, the IURC approved the retirements, including the creation of regulatory assets for the net book value of Units 1 and 2 upon retirement, a method for amortizing those assets, and recovery of the assets through ongoing amortization in future rate cases. The order reserves all parties' rights regarding ratemaking treatment, including the proper rate of return and recovery mechanisms. In December 2021, AES Indiana completed the acquisition of the Hardy Hills Solar Project, a 195 MW solar project expected to commence operations in 2024, which received IURC approval in June 2021. In July 2021, AES Indiana executed an agreement to acquire the Petersburg Solar Project, a 250 MW solar and 180 MWh energy storage facility expected to commence operations in 2025, which also received IURC approval in November 2021. In December 2021 and 2022, AES Indiana received equity capital contributions of $275 million and $253 million, respectively, from AES and CDPQ on a proportional share basis to fund TDSIC and replacement generation projects. AES Ohio is a utility that transmits and distributes electricity to approximately 536,000 retail customers in a 6,000 square mile area of West Central Ohio and is subject to regulatory authority. AES Ohio has the exclusive right to provide transmission and distribution services and procures retail standard service offer (SSO) electric service through a competitive bid auction process. Previously, AES Ohio Generation was a primary subsidiary, but DPL has systematically exited this generation business, retiring and selling its last remaining operating asset in 2020. AES Ohio's financial results are primarily driven by retail demand and weather, as well as regulatory outcomes, changes in legislation or regulations, and timely recovery of transmission and distribution expenditures. AES Ohio is regulated by the PUCO for distribution services, retail rates, reliability, compliance with renewable energy and energy efficiency requirements, and other matters. The PUCO maintains jurisdiction over electricity delivery, SSO, and retail electric services. Customers can purchase power from a Competitive Retail Electric Service (CRES) provider or from their local utility under SSO rates, which are supplied by third parties through competitive bidding. Ohio law requires utilities to file either an Electric Security Plan (ESP) or MRO plan to establish SSO rates. On December 18, 2019, the PUCO approved AES Ohio's Notice of Withdrawal and reversion to its prior rate plan (ESP 1), which reinstated the non-bypassable RSC Rider, generating approximately $79 million in annual revenues. The OCC has appealed to the Ohio Supreme Court, challenging the reversion to ESP 1 and seeking a refund of RSC revenues from August 2021; a decision is pending, and if the appeal results in terms more adverse than the current ESP plan, it could materially affect AES Ohio's results of operations, financial condition, and cash flows. On September 26, 2022, AES Ohio filed its latest ESP ("ESP 4"), a comprehensive plan to upgrade its network, improve service reliability, enhance price stability, and invest in local economic development, including increased distribution infrastructure investments and a proactive vegetation management program. ESP 4 also includes proposals for new customer programs such as renewable options, electric vehicle programs, and energy efficiency initiatives for residential and low-income customers, and seeks to recover outstanding regulatory assets not currently in rates. AES Ohio did not propose continuing the Rate Stabilization Charge in ESP 4, which requires PUCO approval anticipated in 2023. On November 30, 2020, AES Ohio filed a new distribution rate case application with the PUCO to increase base rates to address rising material and labor costs and substantial investments in distribution infrastructure. This increased cost will take effect when AES Ohio has a new electric security plan in place, which is anticipated in 2023. On October 23, 2020, AES Ohio entered into a Stipulation and Recommendation with the PUCO and various customer organizations regarding its Smart Grid Plan, findings that AES Ohio passed the Significantly Excessive Earnings Test (SEET) for 2018 and 2019, and that its current ESP 1 satisfies both the SEET and the more favorable in the aggregate (MFA) regulatory test. In June 2021, the PUCO issued an opinion and order accepting the stipulation as filed, and AES made a $150 million cash contribution in 2021 to improve infrastructure and modernize its grid while maintaining liquidity. Several rehearing applications were filed and denied on December 1, 2021, and the OCC appealed the final PUCO Order to the Ohio Supreme Court on December 6, 2021; this appeal remains pending. On January 23, 2020, AES Ohio filed with the PUCO requesting approval to defer its decoupling costs consistent with the methodology from its Distribution Rate Case; if approved, deferral would be effective December 18, 2019 and would reduce impacts from weather, energy efficiency programs, and changes in customer demand. An evidentiary hearing was held on May 4, 2021, and these amounts are included in the ESP 4 application and are proposed to be recovered in a new rider. AES Ohio plans to spend an estimated $1.2 billion on capital projects from 2023 through 2025, including spending under its Smart Grid Plan from the October 2020 Stipulation and other transmission and distribution projects. The approved Smart Grid Plan provides for a return on and recovery of up to $249 million of Phase 1 investments and recovery of operational and maintenance expenses through the existing Infrastructure Investment Rider for a four-year term, with an aggregate cap of $268 million on recoverable amounts, and acknowledges that AES Ohio may file a subsequent application with the PUCO within three years for Phase 2 of the Smart Grid Plan. These spending programs are contingent on successful regulatory outcomes in pending proceedings. AES Clean Energy, part of AES' U.S. renewables portfolio, is one of the top U.S. renewables growth platforms and offers innovative solutions based on cutting-edge technologies to accelerate customers' energy futures. The generation capacity of systems owned and/or operated under AES Clean Energy is 4,919 MW across the U.S., with 2,862 MW under construction, including 1,707 MW of solar, 639 MW of wind, and 516 MW of energy storage. AES Clean Energy has a 5.2 GW backlog of projects, most expected to come online by 2025. The adoption of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) in 2022 is expected to significantly accelerate U.S. renewables growth, and AES plans to meet this demand with its 51 GW development pipeline. AES Clean Energy comprises AES Renewable Holdings, sPower, AES Clean Energy Development (ACED), and other renewable assets. ACED was formed on February 1, 2021, by merging specifically identified projects from sPower and AES Renewable Holdings, and serves as the development vehicle for all future U.S. renewable projects. Following the merger, ACED expanded through the acquisitions of the Valcour Intermediate Holdings wind platform and Community Energy, a U.S. solar developer. AES Clean Energy has grown organically, now employing more than 1,000 people compared to less than 500 at its formation in 2021, and its development pipeline has more than doubled. In February 2023, the company sold 49% of its indirect interest in a 1.3 GW portfolio of sPower's operating assets ("OpCo B"), including 17 solar projects and one wind project across six states, to Hannon Armstrong Sustainable Infrastructure Capital, Inc. Key financial drivers for AES Clean Energy include efficient construction and operation of renewable facilities under long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), which guarantee energy prices, and substantial tax credits, especially with the IRA. Fuel price fluctuations can alter generation costs and energy prices. Generation businesses with PPAs have mechanisms to recover fuel costs from off-takers, including energy payments based on market fuel prices. When fuel price fluctuations are borne by off-takers, revenue may vary, but the variable margin or profitability remains consistent. Profitability can be influenced by plant efficiency, availability, heat rate, and fuel flexibility. Warrior Run operates as a Qualifying Facility (QF) under PURPA, having entered into a long-term contract with an electric utility that is obligated to purchase power at the utility’s avoided cost—defined as the likely costs of energy and capital investment that would have been incurred if the utility had built or purchased its own generation. To qualify as a QF, a cogeneration facility must produce electricity and useful thermal energy for industrial or commercial processes or heating/cooling applications in specific proportions to its total energy output and meet certain efficiency standards. A small power production facility must generally use a renewable energy input and meet size criteria or be a cogeneration facility that simultaneously generates electricity and process heat or steam. Non-QF U.S. generation businesses currently operate as Exempt Wholesale Generators under the Energy Policy Act of 1992, amending the Public Utility Holding Company Act (PUHCA). These businesses, subject to FERC approval, can sell power at market-based rates directly to the wholesale market or to third-party off-takers such as power marketers or utility/industrial customers. FERC approval to sell wholesale power at market-based rates generally requires demonstrating that the seller lacks market power in generation and transmission, that the seller and its affiliates cannot erect barriers to market entry, and that there are no opportunities for abusive transactions involving regulated affiliates. The U.S. wholesale electricity market consists of multiple regional markets regulated by federal authorities (FERC) and regional organizations (RTOs), which operate regional transmission grids and maintain organized electricity markets. These rules govern the determination of system marginal prices and establish guidelines and incentives for new capacity additions. Electricity supply in Colombia is concentrated in the SIN system, which covers one-third of the country’s territory and provides power to 97% of the population. As of December 31, 2022, the SIN had an installed capacity of 18,771 MW, composed primarily of hydroelectric generation (67%), other renewable sources (3%), and thermal generation (30%). Hydroelectric plants supplied 84% of total energy demand in 2022, and the sector experiences significant price volatility due to seasonal hydrological variations. Colombia’s electricity sector operates under a competitive market for generation and sale, and a regulated framework for transmission and distribution, governed by Colombian laws and the Colombian Regulating Entity for Energy and Gas (CREG). The Ministry of Mines and Energy sets energy policy, the Public Utility Superintendency oversees utility companies, and the Mining and Energy Planning Unit manages expansion planning for generation and transmission. The generation sector operates competitively, with companies selling energy in the wholesale market at short-term prices or through bilateral contracts, and the National Dispatch Center dispatches generators in merit order to meet demand at the lowest cost. System expansion is supported by reliability charge auctions for conventional power plants and long-term energy contract auctions (15 years) for non-conventional renewables. Environmental regulation is governed by Decree 1076 of 2015, which defines the scope of the National Environmental Licensing Authority (ANLA), with additional regulations introduced in 2018 and 2022, including biotic compensation and guidance for environmental studies. AES Colombia has secured environmental licenses for 406 MW of wind projects in its development pipeline. In Argentina, AES operates plants with a total installed capacity of 4,220 MW, representing 10% of the country’s total capacity, featuring a diversified portfolio across wind, hydro, and thermal technologies. The country’s main power system, SADI, serves 96% of the population and had an installed capacity of 42,927 MW as of December 31, 2022, primarily consisting of thermoelectric (59%) and hydroelectric (26%) generation, with wind (8%), nuclear (4%), and solar (3%) contributing to the mix. Thermoelectric generation relies mainly on natural gas, but during winter months (June to August), fuel scarcity due to transport issues leads to the use of oil and coal. Hydrological conditions significantly affect dispatch and market costs, with precipitation occurring from May to October. Argentina’s electricity sector is divided into generation, transmission, and distribution, with the wholesale market involving generation, transmission, distribution companies, and large customers. CAMMESA manages the market and coordinates dispatch, while the Electricity National Regulatory Agency regulates public service and the Secretariat of Energy oversees system framework and grants concessions. A tolling scheme sets prices for electricity and fuel references, making AES particularly sensitive to regulatory changes. The market is structured as an "average cost" system, where generators are compensated for fixed and non-fuel variable costs in Argentine pesos. Renewable expansion is supported by the RenovAr program and private market trading. In the United States, the Clean Air Act (CAA) and state laws regulate emissions of SO₂, NOₓ, particulate matter, greenhouse gases, mercury, and other hazardous air pollutants. The Cross-State Air Pollution Rule (CSAPR) addresses the "good neighbor" provision of the CAA, prohibiting emissions that contribute significantly to other states’ nonattainment of or interference with maintenance of National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). The CSAPR requires significant reductions in SO₂ and NOₓ emissions from power plants in many states where the Company operates, and the Company complies through existing controls and purchases of emissions allowances on the open market. In October 2016, the EPA published a final rule updating the CSAPR to address the 2008 ozone NAAQS (CSAPR Update Rule), finding that NOₓ emissions in 22 states—including Indiana and Maryland and Ohio—interfere with downwind states’ ability to attain and maintain the 2008 ozone NAAQS. The EPA issued federal implementation plans that updated NOₓ emission budgets and modified the allowance trading program, with implementation beginning in the 2017 ozone season and affecting facilities receiving fewer NOₓ allowances starting in 2017. Following legal challenges, on April 30, 2021, the EPA issued the Revised CSAPR Update Rule, requiring affected electric generating units (EGUs) in certain states—including Indiana and Maryland—to participate in a new trading program, the CSAPR NO Ozone Season Group 3 trading program, resulting in fewer NOₓ allowances beginning in 2021, which may require AES facilities to purchase additional allowances. On April 6, 2022, the EPA proposed a Federal Implementation Plan to address air quality impacts related to the 2015 ozone NAAQS, which would establish a revised CSAPR NO Ozone Season Group 3 trading program for 25 states, including Indiana and Maryland, with EGUs beginning to receive fewer allowances as early as 2023, potentially increasing the need to purchase allowances. While the Company’s additional CSAPR compliance costs to date have been immaterial, the future availability and cost of allowances to meet emission reduction requirements are uncertain and could become material if facilities need to purchase more allowances. The New Source Review (NSR) requirements under the CAA impose obligations on major emission sources, such as electric generating stations, if changes result in a significant increase in emissions. Projects like power plant modifications may be excluded from NSR if they qualify under the routine maintenance, repair, and replacement (RMRR) exclusion. There is ongoing litigation and uncertainty about which projects fall under the RMRR exclusion. The EPA has filed lawsuits against coal-fired power plant owners and issued Notices of Violation (NOVs) to several owners alleging NSR violations. An NOV was issued by the EPA against AES Indiana concerning NSR and prevention of significant deterioration under the CAA. If NSR requirements are imposed on any of the Company’s subsidiaries’ power plants, it could have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, financial condition, and results of operations. The AES Corporation is a registered electric holding company under the PUHCA 2005, enacted as part of the EPAct 2005. PUHCA 2005 removed many restrictions from the U.S. Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 while maintaining FERC and state utility commissions’ access to certain utility holding companies’ books and records. It also creates new challenges and opportunities by easing barriers to mergers and combinations, increasing the likelihood of large, geographically dispersed utility holding companies with greater financial strength and competitive capacity. Other provisions of the EPAct 2005 allow FERC to eliminate PURPA purchase/sale obligations from utilities if there are sufficient opportunities to sell into competitive markets. FERC has applied this authority with a rebuttable presumption that utilities within the control areas of MISO, PJM, ISO New England, Inc., the New York Independent System Operator, Inc., and ERCOT are not required to purchase or sell power from or to qualified facilities (QFs) above a certain size. FERC may also remove purchase/sale obligations on a case-by-case basis. There is no U.S. federal law mandating GHG emission reductions for power generation, though in 2015, the EPA established New Source Performance Standards for CO₂ emissions from new or modified fossil-fueled steam units over 25 MW, and in 2018 proposed revisions. In 2019, the EPA issued the Affordable Clean Energy (ACE) Rule, which set heat rate improvements as the best system for reducing emissions from existing coal plants. On January 19, 2021, the D.C. Circuit vacated and remanded the ACE Rule to the EPA, with a partial stay granted on February 22, 2021, and a partial mandate issued on March 5, 2021, effectively nullifying the ACE Rule. On October 29, 2021, the U.S. Supreme Court granted petitions to review the D.C. Circuit’s decision, and on June 30, 2022, reversed the D.C. Circuit’s judgment, remanding the case for further proceedings and holding that the “generation shifting” approach in the Clean Power Plan (CPP) exceeded EPA’s authority under Section 111(d) of the CAA. As a result, on October 27, 2022, the D.C. Circuit recalled its March 5, 2021 mandate and issued a new partial mandate holding challenges to the ACE Rule in abeyance while the EPA develops a replacement Section 111(d) rule. For each transaction, it must determine whether the transaction impacts its consolidation conclusion by first assessing whether the transaction should be evaluated under the variable interest model or the voting model. In determining which model applies, the Company makes judgments about how the entity operates, including whether (i) the entity has sufficient equity to finance its activities, (ii) the equity holders, as a group, have the characteristics of a controlling financial interest, and (iii) the entity has non-substantive voting rights. If the entity is a variable interest entity, the most significant judgment is whether the Company, including its related parties and de facto agents, collectively have power and benefits. If AES has power and benefits, the entity will be consolidated by AES. Alternatively, if the entity is a voting model entity, the key judgments involve determining whether non-AES shareholders have substantive participating rights. Assessing shareholder rights and whether they are substantive participating rights requires significant judgment, as such rights may include selecting, terminating, or setting management compensation and establishing operating and capital decisions, including budgets, in the ordinary course of business. Conversely, if shareholder rights are only protective in nature (referred to as protective rights), they do not override the presumption that the owner of a majority voting interest consolidates its investee. Significant judgment is required to determine whether minority rights represent substantive participating rights or protective rights that do not affect the control evaluation. While both types of rights involve approval or veto power, a distinguishing factor is the underlying activity or action to which the right relates. Pension and Other Postretirement Plans — The Company recognizes a net asset or liability reflecting the funded status of pension and other postretirement plans, with current-year changes in actuarial gains or losses recognized in AOCL, except for those plans at certain regulated utilities that can recover portions of their pension and postretirement obligations through future rates. The valuation of the benefit obligation, fair value of plan assets, and net periodic benefit costs requires various estimates and assumptions, the most significant of which are the discount rate and expected return on plan assets. These assumptions are reviewed annually. Refer to Note 1—General and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies included in Item 8 of this Form 10-K for further information. Revenue Recognition — The Company recognizes revenue to reflect the transfer of energy, capacity, and other services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration to which it expects to be entitled. In applying the revenue model, it determines whether the sale of energy, capacity, and other services represents a single performance obligation based on individual market and contract terms. Generally, the promise to transfer energy and capacity represents a performance obligation satisfied over time and meets the criteria to be accounted for as a series of distinct goods or services. Progress toward satisfaction is measured using output methods, such as MWhs delivered or MWs made available, and when the Company is entitled to consideration corresponding directly to the value of performance completed to date, revenue is recognized in the amount to which it has the right to invoice. The information in this document outlines various risks affecting AES's financial performance, including commodity price risk, foreign exchange rate risk, and interest rate risks. Commodity price risk arises because some generation businesses operate under short-term sales, have contracted obligations exceeding supply, or rely on imperfect fuel pass-throughs, exposing them to volatility in electricity, fuel, and environmental credit prices. To manage this risk, AES uses physical and financial contracts, futures, swaps, and options, particularly locking in spreads per MWh between variable costs and electricity sales prices. For 2023, AES projects a $5 million gain for power, a $10 million loss for oil, and a $5 million loss for coal and natural gas on a 10% (uncorrelated) move in commodity prices, excluding any correlation between oil and coal or natural gas. Downside exposure occurs with lower power, lower oil, higher natural gas, and higher coal prices, and these exposures vary by business and change as new contracts or hedges are executed. Local market factors such as hydrology, supply/demand balances, fuel supply, competition, bidding strategies, and regulatory interventions influence sensitivities, which are not perfectly linear or symmetric. Operational flexibility and volume variations—driven by weather and economic conditions—also affect exposure. In the US and Utilities SBU, generation businesses are largely contracted but may retain residual risk if contracts are not perfectly indexed to business drivers. Southland’s legacy assets operate through the end of 2023 and have seen increased energy revenue from capacity contracts. In South America, Chile’s assets in central and northern regions have PPAs with coal-indexed prices, and non-indexed contracts are hedged using international coal instruments for up to three years. Colombia operates with spot market exposure due to short-term sales and lacks fuel-indexed contracts, while Brazil’s hydroelectric facility is covered by contracts, and under drier conditions, spot purchases may be needed due to insufficient regulated sharing. In MCAC, Panama is exposed to hydrology-based variance and spot prices influenced by oil and natural gas, and the Dominican Republic’s natural gas plants face commodity-linked price movements with mismatched contract and generation availability, leading to spot market positions as buyers or sellers. In Eurasia, Vietnam and Bulgaria have minimal commodity exposure due to lack of merchant activity and fuel pass-through mechanisms. Foreign exchange risk stems from operations in foreign subsidiaries and affiliates using currencies other than USD, with exposure to the Argentine peso, Brazilian real, Chilean peso, Colombian peso, Dominican peso, Euro, and Mexican peso. The largest risks in 2023 are from the Brazilian real and Euro. Assuming a 10% USD appreciation as of December 31, 2022, cash distributions from subsidiaries exposed to these currencies are projected to experience less than a $10 million gain for the Brazilian real, less than a $5 million gain for the Colombian peso, and less than a $5 million loss for the Euro, net of hedges and holding other variables constant. These sensitivities are based on forecasted cash distributions and may change with new hedges or unwound positions, and do not account for administrative market restrictions or currency inconvertibility. Interest rate risk arises from variable and fixed-rate debt and interest rate swap, cap, floor, and option agreements. Financing decisions align with individual business or plant risk factors, and fixed or variable-rate financing is used to hedge interest rate fluctuations. In some cases, particularly with non-recourse financing, interest rate swaps, caps, and floors are used to fix or limit interest rate exposure. Most of AES’s interest rate risk is related to these financing arrangements.

The company is exposed to foreign exchange risk due to its subsidiaries holding debt denominated in the Argentine peso, Brazilian real, Chilean peso, Colombian peso, Euro, and USD, with sensitivities presented net of outstanding hedges and assuming all other variables remain constant. These sensitivities reflect net exposure after transactional gains or losses and may change in the future due to new hedging activities or unwinding of existing hedges, as well as updates to forecasted cash distributions exposed to foreign exchange risk. The sensitivities do not account for administrative market restrictions or currency inconvertibility. Regarding interest rate risk, the company faces exposure from variable and fixed-rate debt, as well as interest rate swap, cap, floor, and option agreements. The mix of fixed and variable-rate debt is determined based on the risk profile of individual businesses or plants, with fixed-rate financing used to hedge against interest rate fluctuations when revenue or capacity payments are fixed or inflation-sensitive. In non-recourse financing cases, the company uses interest rate swaps, caps, and floors to fix or limit interest rate exposure. Most of the interest rate risk stems from non-recourse financings at its businesses. As of December 31, 2022, the portfolio’s pre-tax earnings exposure for 2023 to a one-time 100-basis-point increase in interest rates for debt denominated in the Argentine peso, Brazilian real, Chilean peso, Colombian peso, Euro, and USD would be less than $55 million in interest expense. These figures do not consider the historical correlation between these interest rates. The audit compared management’s assumptions to current industry and economic trends and historical performance. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess how changes in assumptions would affect fair value. Valuation specialists were engaged to assist in evaluating the overall valuation methodology and the discount rates used in fair value estimates. AES recognizes adjustments to the carrying value of equity instruments that are currently redeemable or where it is probable they will become redeemable by reducing retained earnings or additional paid-in capital, if retained earnings are not available; such adjustments are classified as temporary equity. If the equity instrument is not probable of becoming redeemable, no adjustment to carrying value is made. Mandatorily redeemable instruments are classified as liabilities. Investments in entities over which the Company has significant influence but not control are accounted for using the equity method and reported under Investments in and advances to affiliates on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. The Company’s proportionate share of net income or loss is included in Net equity in losses of affiliates on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. To determine whether distributions from equity method investees are returns of investment or returns on investment, the Company uses the cumulative earnings approach. The equity method is discontinued when an investment is reduced to zero and the Company has no further commitment to support the investee, and it is resumed when net income exceeds previously unrecorded shares of net losses. Upon acquiring an investment, the Company determines the fair value of identifiable assets and assumed liabilities, and the basis difference between fair value and carrying amount is amortized over the life of the asset or liability, with AES’s share recognized in Net equity in losses of affiliates. The Company periodically evaluates equity method investments for impairment indicators; when impairment is observed and deemed other-than-temporary, the excess of carrying amount over estimated fair value is recognized as an expense in Other non-operating expense. Acquisitions and disposals of business interests are generally treated as consolidated businesses, assets, or equity method investments. Losses on expected sales are limited to the impairment of long-lived assets as of the sales agreement date and are recognized in Asset impairment expense. Gains or losses upon completion of disposals, including reclassification of cumulative translation adjustments, are recognized in Loss on disposal and sale of business interests upon sale completion. For certain U.S. renewable generation partnerships with profit-sharing arrangements not based on fixed ownership percentages, the Company uses the hypothetical liquidation at book value (HLBV) method, which calculates proceeds each partner would receive if the partnership were liquidated at book value at the balance sheet date. Each partner’s share of income is the change in their legally claimable net equity based on the HLBV, adjusted for capital transactions. The HLBV method is applied both to allocate equity earnings to AES when the renewable business is accounted for under the equity method and to calculate earnings attributable to noncontrolling interest when the business is consolidated. In the early months of operation of a renewable facility, if HLBV results in a significant decrease in the hypothetical liquidation proceeds to the tax equity investor due to investment tax credits or other U.S. Internal Revenue Code adjustments, the Company records the impact—referred to as the ‘Day one gain’—in the same period. A disposal group classified as held-for-sale is reported at the lower of carrying amount or estimated fair value less cost to sell. A loss is recognized if carrying amount exceeds estimated fair value less cost to sell, limited to the carrying value of long-lived assets until sale completion, after which any additional loss is recognized. If fair value exceeds carrying amount while still held-for-sale, previously recognized impairment expenses are reversed up to the lesser of the previously recognized amount or the subsequent excess. Assets and liabilities of held-for-sale disposal groups are segregated in the current balance sheet when classified as held-for-sale and are classified as current if expected to be disposed of within twelve months. Transactions between the held-for-sale group and continuing businesses are not eliminated to reflect ongoing operations. Discontinued operations are reported separately when the disposal of a business or group represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations and financial results. Cash flows from discontinued operations are included in the relevant categories of operating, investing, and financing activities. Results of discontinued operations include gains or losses from closing or adjusting carrying amounts to fair value less cost to sell, including gains or losses related to noncontrolling interests upon disposal. The Company determines the fair value of financial assets and liabilities using fair value measurement guidance, applying it to marketable debt and equity securities classified in Short-term investments and Other noncurrent assets, derivative assets in Other current assets and Other noncurrent assets, and derivative liabilities in Accrued and other liabilities (current) and Other noncurrent liabilities. The guidance is also applied to nonfinancial assets and liabilities upon business or asset acquisition by a variable interest entity, or in assessing asset retirement obligations or potential impairments related to asset groups, equity method investments, or goodwill. Fair value is based on the exit price in an orderly, hypothetical transaction between market participants at the measurement date, considering the principal or most advantageous market and market participant assumptions such as inherent risk, transfer restrictions, and risk of nonperformance. Transaction costs and blockage factors are excluded. The Company prioritizes observable inputs over unobservable ones and classifies assets and liabilities into three levels of the fair value hierarchy: Level 1 uses quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities; Level 2 includes observable inputs such as quoted prices in active or inactive markets for similar assets or liabilities or other corroborated observable data; Level 3 involves unobservable inputs with little or no market activity. Transfers between levels are recognized at the end of the reporting period. Finite-lived intangible assets are amortized over their useful lives, which range from 1 to 50 years, and are included in the Consolidated Balance Sheet under the line item "Other intangible assets." Events such as adverse regulatory changes, unfavorable power or fuel prices, increased grid competition, technological advancements, declining demand, or an expectation of early disposal may trigger such evaluations. If the carrying amount exceeds undiscounted cash flows, an impairment expense is recognized for the excess over fair value, subject to not reducing the carrying amount below fair value for individual assets where fair value is determinable without undue cost or effort. Impairment expenses for certain assets may be reduced by the establishment of a regulatory asset if recovery through approved rates is probable. Debt issuance costs are deferred and presented as a direct reduction from the face amount of long-term debt, amortized over the financing period using the effective interest method; for line-of-credit or revolving credit facilities, these costs are deferred as an asset and amortized over the financing period. Make-whole payments upon early debt retirement are classified as cash flows used in financing activities. Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets are evaluated for impairment annually on October 1st or whenever events or changes in circumstances require such evaluation. Goodwill, representing the excess of purchase price over the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired, is assigned to reporting units expected to benefit from acquisition synergies, with each AES business having goodwill constituting a separate reporting unit due to differences in operations and segment reporting. Goodwill is assessed either through a qualitative or quantitative test to determine the fair value of the reporting unit; if impaired, an impairment loss is recorded equal to the amount by which the reporting unit’s carrying amount exceeds its fair value, not exceeding the carrying amount of goodwill. Indefinite-lived intangible assets, primarily land-use and water rights, are evaluated similarly, and if their carrying amount exceeds fair value, the excess is recognized as an impairment expense. Accounts payable consist of amounts owed to trade creditors for energy, fuel, maintenance, inventory, and other raw materials related to core operations. Other accrued liabilities include $662 million from supplier financing arrangements, of which $296 million is guaranteed by the Parent Company; interest on these arrangements is recorded in Interest Expense or, if eligible, to Property, Plant and Equipment, Net. The remainder of other accrued liabilities includes income taxes, regulatory liabilities, legal contingencies, and employee-related costs such as payroll and benefits. Regulatory assets represent incurred costs deferred for probable future recovery through customer rates and are reflected in Interest Income; regulatory liabilities represent obligations to refund customers. Management assesses the probability of recovery or payment based on regulatory changes, rate orders, and pending deregulation legislation; if future recovery is no longer probable, the related regulatory asset is written off and recognized in income from continuing operations. Pension and other postretirement plans are reflected in the Consolidated Balance Sheets based on their funded status, with current-year actuarial gains or losses recognized in AOCL, except for plans at regulated utilities where portions of obligations can be recovered through future rates. All plan assets are recorded at fair value, and AES follows the year-end measurement date requirement for defined benefit plans. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognized for future tax consequences of temporary differences between financial statement carrying amounts and tax bases; a valuation allowance is established when it is more likely than not that all or part of a deferred tax asset will not be realized. Tax positions are evaluated under a more likely than not threshold before recognition. Uncertain tax positions are classified as noncurrent income tax liabilities unless expected to be paid within one year. Interest and penalties related to income tax exposures are recognized as part of the provision for income taxes. The Company treats GILTI as an expense in the period it is accrued, resulting in no deferred tax assets or liabilities related to GILTI. The investment tax credit is accounted for using the flow-through method. Income tax effects from AOCL are released on a portfolio basis. The Company has elected not to consider the corporate alternative minimum tax in future periods when assessing the realizability of deferred tax assets, carryforwards, or tax credits, and any impact on realization is recognized in the period it arises. Asset retirement obligations are recorded at fair value when incurred, with the cost capitalized by increasing the carrying amount of the related long-lived asset; the liability is accreted to present value each period, and the capitalized cost is depreciated over the asset’s useful life. Upon settlement, the liability is eliminated, and a gain or loss is recognized based on the actual retirement cost. Foreign currency translation adjustments arising from the translation of subsidiaries' balance sheets are included in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss (AOCL). Revenue and expense accounts of subsidiaries and affiliates are translated into U.S. dollars using the average exchange rates for the period. Gains and losses on long-term intercompany foreign currency transactions that the Company does not intend to settle in the foreseeable future are also recognized in AOCL. Gains and losses from exchange rate fluctuations on transactions denominated in a currency other than the functional currency are included in net income. Accumulated foreign currency translation adjustments are reclassified from AOCL to net income only when realized through the sale of a foreign entity or upon complete or substantially complete liquidation of the investment in that entity. These accumulated adjustments are included in carrying amounts during impairment assessments when the Company has committed to a plan that will result in their reclassification to earnings. Revenue is recognized when control of promised goods or services is transferred to customers, reflecting the consideration the Company expects to receive. Revenue is recorded net of taxes assessed on and collected from customers, which are remitted to governmental authorities. Utilities sell electricity directly to end-users and bill customers directly; most utility contracts have a single performance obligation because energy, capacity, and distribution/transmission services are not distinct, and since the performance obligation is satisfied over time with a consistent method of measuring progress, it qualifies as a series. Utility revenue is classified as regulated on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. Utility businesses are subject to government regulation, which sets tariffs for electricity prices, directly aligning the utility’s billing rights with the customer value of the services provided each period. Month-to-month contracts use an output method based on megawatt-hours (MWh) delivered each month, measured at the approved tariff. The Company purchases power to meet customer demand not covered by separate power purchase agreements (PPAs) and accounts for these transactions on a net hourly basis due to net hourly settlements. In limited cases, a utility customer may choose a third-party provider, and the Company may act as a billing agent, recognizing revenue on a net basis. Generation contracts, depending on market conditions and contract terms, may have one or more performance obligations, as the transfer of energy, capacity, or other services may be distinct. For contracts with multiple performance obligations, revenue is allocated based on relative standalone selling prices using a market or expected cost plus margin approach. Variable consideration is allocated to one or more, but not all, distinct goods or services within a single performance obligation if (1) it relates specifically to efforts to transfer the good or service, and (2) it reflects the amount the Company expects to receive for transferring the promised good or service. If a contract includes a capacity-related performance obligation, it is generally satisfied over time and qualifies as a series if the same method is used to measure progress. Progress is measured using the "right to invoice" practical expedient when available, and revenue is recognized for the amount the Company has a right to receive, corresponding directly to the value of performance completed. Revenue from generation businesses is classified as non-regulated. Energy performance obligations are recognized using an output method, as energy delivered best reflects the transfer of goods or services. Energy delivery generally satisfies the performance obligation. In certain contracts, if plant availability exceeds a contractual target, the Company receives a performance bonus; if availability falls below a guaranteed minimum, a non-availability penalty is incurred. These bonuses or penalties are variable consideration and are estimated and recognized when it is probable there will not be a significant reversal. Some generation contracts include operating or sales-type leases where capacity payments are considered lease elements, and the allocation between lease and non-lease components is made at lease inception under ASC 842. The Company evaluates the nature of the promise and legally enforceable rights in the contract to determine whether variable quantities represent variable consideration or an option to acquire additional goods or services. In requirement contracts, the customer’s right to purchase additional goods or services is distinct, resulting in a new obligation, and the variable quantities are considered an option. When energy or capacity is sold or purchased in the spot market or to ISOs, the Company assesses facts and circumstances to determine whether spot revenues and purchases should be presented gross or net. Generally, a generator is either a net seller or net buyer on an hourly basis, and revenue is recognized for net seller hours and cost of sales for net buyer hours. The transaction price allocated to a construction performance obligation is recognized over time as construction occurs, with full revenue recognition upon completion. A timing difference between revenue recognition and cash collection may result in a significant financing component, which is accounted for under the effective interest rate method, resulting in a long-term receivable recorded in the Loan Receivable line item on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. As payments are collected, the consideration is bifurcated between principal repayment of the long-term receivable and interest income, recognized in the Consolidated Statements of Operations. Contract balances result from differences in timing between revenue recognition, billings, and cash collections. The Company has elected to apply optional disclosure exemptions under ASC 606, so the amount disclosed in Note 20—Revenue excludes contracts with an original length of one year or less, contracts for which revenue is recognized based on the amount the Company has the right to invoice for services performed, and variable consideration allocated entirely to a wholly unsatisfied performance obligation when the consideration relates specifically to the Company’s efforts to satisfy the performance obligation and reflects the amount to which it expects to be entitled. Estimates of revenue expected to be recognized in future periods also exclude unexercised customer options to purchase additional goods or services that do not represent material rights to the customer. The Company has operating and finance leases for energy production facilities, land, office space, transmission lines, vehicles, and other operating equipment in which it is the lessee. Operating leases with an initial term of 12 months or less are not recorded on the balance sheet but are expensed on a straight-line basis over the lease term. The leases do not contain material residual value guarantees or restrictive covenants or subleases. Right-of-use assets represent the Company’s right to use an underlying asset for the lease term, while lease liabilities represent its obligation to make lease payments. These are recognized on lease commencement based on the present value of lease payments over the lease term. Since the rate implicit in the lease is not readily determinable, the Company uses the subsidiaries’ incremental borrowing rate, based on information available at commencement, to determine the present value of lease payments. Discount rates are derived from the Company’s existing credit rates on unsecured borrowings, adjusted for the appropriate lease term and currency. The right-of-use asset includes any lease payments made but excludes lease incentives paid or payable at commencement. The lease term includes the option to extend or terminate the lease if it is reasonably certain that the option will be exercised. The Company has operating leases for certain generation contracts that include provisions to provide capacity to a customer, a stand-ready obligation to deliver energy when required, in which it is the lessor. Capacity payments are generally considered lease elements as they cover the majority of available output from a facility. The allocation of contract payments between lease and non-lease elements occurs at lease inception. Fixed lease payments from such contracts are recognized as lease revenue on a straight-line basis over the lease term, while variable lease payments are recognized when earned. The Company has sales-type leases for battery energy storage systems (BESS) in which it is the lessor. These arrangements allow customers to determine when to charge and discharge the BESS, representing a transfer of control and constitute the arrangement as a sales-type lease. Upon lease commencement, the book value of the leased asset is removed from the balance sheet, and a net investment in a sales-type lease is recognized based on the present value of fixed payments under the contract and the residual value of the underlying asset. The Company grants share-based compensation in the form of restricted stock units, performance stock units, performance cash units, and stock options. Expense is based on the grant-date fair value of the equity or liability instrument and is recognized on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period, net of estimated forfeitures. The Company uses a Black-Scholes option pricing model to estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees. General and administrative expenses include corporate and other expenses related to corporate staff functions and initiatives, primarily executive management, finance, legal, human resources, and information systems, which are not directly allocable to business segments. Additionally, all costs associated with corporate business development efforts are classified as general and administrative expenses. Under the accounting standards for derivatives and hedging, the Company recognizes all contracts that meet the definition of a derivative, except those designated as normal purchase or normal sale at inception, as either assets or liabilities in the Consolidated Balance Sheets and measures them at fair value. PPAs and fuel supply agreements are evaluated to determine if they contain a derivative or an embedded derivative requiring separate valuation and accounting. Generally, these agreements do not meet the definition of a derivative due to the inability to be net settled. On a quarterly basis, the Company evaluates the markets for commodities to be delivered under these agreements to determine if facts and circumstances have changed such that the agreements could be net settled and meet the definition of a derivative. The Company typically designates its derivative instruments as cash flow hedges if they meet the criteria specified in ASC 815, Derivatives and Hedging. It enters into interest rate swap agreements to hedge the variability of expected future cash interest payments and uses foreign currency contracts to reduce risks arising from changes in the fair value of certain foreign currency-denominated assets and liabilities. The objective of these practices is to minimize the impact of foreign currency fluctuations on operating results
